THE VIGILANTS AT HARRISON.
Between 8 and 9 o'clock Friday night, while attending a meeting of the temperance choir, we were startled by a terrific firing near the public square, and immediately rushed down to ascertain the cause. Citizens whom we met seemed to be in a general panic, and it was plait apparent that something of a fearful nature had occurred. After some general inquiry, we proceeded, in company with Marshal I. R. Moore, to the open place on Stephenson avenue, where we found his son Bob and Geo. Cotten leaning over the dead body of Wm. Arterberry, who is spoken of as being charged with incendiarism. The sight was a fearful one, his face gory and exhibiting, even in death, the intense fear and desperation which must have taken possession of him. On closer inspection, we found on his breast a card inscribed as follows:

"Outlaws Take Warning!!

No more Burning!

No more Pistol Shooting!

No more selling liquor without license!

Behave yourselves or tremble, your fate is sealed!!! VIGILANTS."

At first we were unable to find the guards, they having been taken some distance by the perpetrators of this awful deed; but, after some time, they returned, and told particulars somewhat as follows:

The prisoner and guards had taken supper at the Miles hotel, and were returning down town, when, just as they had arrived opposite the old parsonage, they were halted by a number of mounted men, and immediately surrounded by overpowering numbers. The guards, who were especially selected by our worthy sheriff as men of known bravery and coolness, drew their weapons, but were unable to accomplish anything, so alert were the assaulting parties. A blanket was thrown over the head of one, a cocked pistol foreed in the mouth of another, while a third was felled to the ground with some heavy weapon in the hands of a vigilant.

The prisoner was seized and marched off, evidently for the purpose of hanging, but he certainly proved too much for his would-be executors, and was about to escape, when shots innumerable were fired at him, all seeming to enter at his back except one, which was planted in the center of his forehead. * * * The vigilants were all masked or blacked, and as but few words were spoken, the guards were unable to recognize a single individual. Some suggest that a portion of them were from Marion county, where the prisoner was charged with murder several years ago; others, that citizens of our town and county, becoming alarmed at the danger to public buildings, had felt themselves forced to form this dangerous organization and take this fearful step. Be this as it may, the affair is a terrible one, and should be deplored by every good citizen. It will add another blot to our already darkened reputation, and we cannot but think that this man could have been better punished in a legal manner. Let us devoutly hope that Harrison will never again suffer from the visitations of the "vigilants."—Harrison Times, Oct. 30.

Cotton is falling and collections short—and Garfield is elected. Garfield and Authur are elected; Hancock and English defeated. The solid south voted for Hancock, together with New Jersey and Nevada. The "balance" of the states went for Garfield. An old negro woman was burned to death in Little Rock, on the 5th. It is supposed that she set fire to her cabin in a drunken freak.
The Kellogg Printing Company, will commence the publication of a periodical styed the Arkansas School Journal. A long needed want supplied.

The negro, Rush Bennett, who killed Col. Jameson of Union county in in the spring of 1879 was convicted of murder in the first degree and condemned to be hung on the 4th of February next—at the last term of Union county circuit court

Boone county had a little fun last week. A man named William Arterberry set the county jail on fire, and seventy-five disguised and armed men overpowered the guards and killed the prisoner. You should build another jail, put those seventy-five men therein, give them a fair trial and then hang them for murder.

"Pears to me your mill goes awful slow," said an impatient farmer boy to a miller; "I could eat that meal faster'n you grind it." How long do you think you could do it, my ladl" quoth the miller. "Till I starved to death," answered the boy.

A small appropriation from the coming legislature to be used in scattering information as to the wonderful inducements which Arkansas presents to home seekers, would prove a most valuable investment. It is certainly time a beginnig in this direction should be made.—Democrat.

The south must rely more upon itself. Its fortunes are in its own hands. If it hopes to win in the great struggle of life, it must keep up, enlarge and improve its public schools; it must raise all the horses, mules, cattle, hogs and sheep it needs; it must raise its wheat and corn and build mills to grind them up; it must build manufactories and convert its cotton into cloth. In a word, it must help itself and not attempt to live by exporting cotton and buying abroad everything it needs and consumes.—[Gazette.

There is some talk outside of Texas about the State being divided up into about four or five smaller States. It is apprehended that the people of Texas will put in a veto if they are consulted on the subject. The proposed division would create the necessity for more legislatures, more office-holders, and a general increase of taxation; hence the average taxpayer will regard the division movement with as much dread as did the Yankee the man at the dinner table, who shoveled in food with his knife. "For God's sake, stranger, don't make that hole in your face any bigger, or we will all starve to death." Texas is not yearning for either an increase in officials or in Texas. Those already enjoyed are ample for all purposes [Texarkana Democrat.

Not the least important of the duties of the legislature which assembles in January, will be a revision of much of the work of its immediate predecessor. The act which repealed the act providing for the publication of the lands delinquent for taxes in the several counties should be repealed, and the old system adopted. The act relating to the assessment and collection of the revenues should receive early and thoughtful attention. It is claimed, and probably not without a show of reason, that unjust and uneous discriminations are made. The code of practice needs revision in order to meet the demands of our increasing population, and the growing wants of the business community. The action of the next legislature will be watched with no uncommon interest, and if the members but set themselves to work in earnest, instead of fritting away their time in useless bickerings and ridiculous borebest, they will earn and receive the grateful thanks of the people.—Juanette.
